content:
San Felice is one of our favorite Italian wine producers, the brand creating a wide range of wines from throughout Tuscany — though primarily Chianti Classico.

Today we look at five 2026 releases from the producer, all excellent and well worth your while.

2024 San Felice In Avane Chardonnay Toscana IGT – A new wine to me, this is a rather brooding expression of chardonnay. The restrained offering finds itself a bit bitter on the attack, notes of lime leaf tucking in to underripe apple, white florals, and lemon curd as the palate develops. The expected breakthrough into more exuberant fruitiness along with some salinity on the finish never really arrives, the affair stopping short before it feels like things really get going. Flashes of interest, however. B+ / $40

2023 San Felice Borgo Chianti Classico DOCG – Iconic Chianti, this offers a bright, cherry-fueled attack that is laced through and through with green herbs, hints of anise, and some dark chocolate. Ample acidity keeps the wine lively and refreshing, with citrusy notes developing as the finish approaches. There’s lemon and orange peel here, evoking thoughts of mostarda and cut grass. Quite versatile and lovely throughout. A- / $40

2022 San Felice Pugnitello Toscana IGT – Punchy and driven by tobacco and dark chocolate notes, San Felice (which is one of the premiere developers of pugnitello) has refined this grape to showcase its more savory characteristics — heavy on licorice, tobacco, light touches of tar — while simultaneously allowing fruit to peek through the cracks. Black cherry, blackberry, and late-game rhubarb all offer a juicy but almost wintry quality to the wine, though intense acidity and more moderated tannins keep everything both tight and lively. I’d hold this for a few years just to see what happens. A- / $95

2022 San Felice Il Grigio Chianti Classico Riserva DOCG – Surprisingly more fruit-forward than expected for a Riserva level Chianti Classico, this unabashedly cherry-fueled offers gentle tertiary notes of cloves and a touch of black tea, before a brighter raspberry-fueled finish comes into focus. Any licorice notes on the finish are more candied, fitting in perfectly with the theme to date. A- / $37

2021 San Felice Campogiovanni Brunello di Montalcino DOCG – A thick and slightly raisiny wine with chocolate overtones, this Brunello leans richer than is typical, its cherry and wild berry notes comparatively muted. Dark caramel and even more chocolate notes build from there, leading to a gravelly charcoal and toasty anise conclusion. The overtly oxidized sweetness, almost date-lake, becomes thick on the finish, finding a foil in a heavy layer of vanilla. The palate ends up all but coated with the extracted, almost jammy character. A bit too heavy for me. B+ / $80

2022 San Felice La Pieve Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG – As with Borgo, this presents a classic Chianti structure — tightly wound cherry, layered tannins, and modest spice to even it all out. The anise is lightened up, which lets the chocolate character fire more freely, notes of graphite and turned earth both becoming prominent as the finish emerges. For all its depth of flavor, the wine is surprisingly straightforward, never deviating from its mission, though the cherry turns more toward blackberry on the lengthy, exuberant, and wholly enjoyable finish. Sometimes, a seamless through-line works out just fine. A / $95

content:
New Riff Distillery hasn’t been slowing down one bit. They recently completed a significant expansion at their Newport, Kentucky distillery, increasing production capacity by 50%, and they’ve added the necessary barrel warehousing at a nearby site. They also increased their distribution footprint to include whiskey-hungry Florida and Illinois. And they remain, as ever, dedicated to making what they call “whiskey riffs.” The latest, however, is actually a riff on a riff. I’ll let them explain:

“Last year we released our Malted Rye Whiskey, and experiencing its remarkably elegant, sophisticated character gave us another idea,” said co-founder Jay Erisman. “We think of it as a malt whiskey first and a rye whiskey second, which raised the question: what would happen if we treated it like other malt whiskies and aged it in sherry casks?”

New Riff’s first batches of 100% Malted Rye Whiskey were distilled in 2014, and the initial release landed in May 2021. For this sherry finished elaboration, New Riff imported custom-made 53-gallon Spanish sherry casks and filled them with 5-year-old New Riff Malted Rye Whiskey. Twelve oloroso and three Pedro Ximenez casks were filled with whiskey and aged another year, before being vatted in the fall of 2021 and left to marry and condition together for several following months until they were bottled in spring of 2022 (at cask strength).

The distillery has put out no shortage of winning “riffs” in recent years, including the malted rye at the heart of this expression. Let’s see how the latest edition stacks up.

Update: We’re adding fresh coverage of this re-released whiskey to expand this review.

New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (2022) Review

The sherry finishing and higher proof have definitely added some heft to the aroma compared to the standard malted rye with ample spice cabinet and leathery notes of dark berries and sweet almond paste. The sherry isn’t overpowering though, and things remain fairly wood-driven with cinnamon stick and toasty barrel char growing more prominent as it opens in the glass. The palate showcases even more sweet sherry character with bold, syrupy notes of blackberry cobbler and raspberry candies. The rye spice is unusually a bit more prominent than in the original, with black pepper and clove popping on the mid-palate and segueing to a generous finish of cooked red fruits, some mild oaky astringency, and lingering notes of tobacco and cherry juice.

Like past limited editions, this bottle was made available only to New Riff’s Whiskey Club and select retailers. However, the success of Malted Rye last year has landed it in the New Riff core lineup, so perhaps we will be seeing even more of this sherry-finished expression in the future. 112.7 proof. A- / $65 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (2026) Review

A few small changes: The previous release started with 5-year-old malted rye and this year’s whiskey started as 6-year-old malted rye. Both were finished in oloroso and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks. Both hit the bottle at cask strength but this year’s release is 2.5% stronger.

The nose of this reissued offering is big and sings both rye and sherry notes at full volume. Raisin and cinnamon sticks hit first, wrapped in leather. Raspberry compote comes next along with caramel and some clove. A touch of cereal grain follows through at the end.

Sipped neat, the whiskey hits hard. In his review four years ago, Drew noted that the rye spices are bolder in this finished whiskey than they are in the unfinished rye, and that is absolutely still the case in the newest release. Sharp cinnamon, fresh cracked black pepper, and clove come bursting out of the glass along with an alcohol bite. Immediately following come sherry notes including raspberry preserves, blackberry, and caramel. Midpalate brings some vanilla to the mix, which stays through the long finish. The good folks at New Riff recommend adding water to bring out the sherry notes or abstaining to highlight the rye. I gave both a try, and it’s true, but the rye notes never disappeared with the addition of water.

Altogether, this a well crafted whiskey that deserves serious attention from fans of both rye whiskey and sherry-finished single malts. -RL 117.3 proof. A- / $70

content:
Not a typo. “Kentucke County,” with an “e,” is the name of the product. It’s a new sub-label from 15 Stars, which has been spinning off other “Kentucky heritage” brands like First West of late, with two expressions available at launch. (“Both in commemorative, collectible bottles,” presumably because of the “250th anniversary” sticker below the front label.)

What’s this Kentucke all about?

In 1776, the same year the American colonies declared their independence, Kentucke County was established as Virginia’s western frontier county. The region would later evolve into the Kentucke District, within which Bourbon County was created, and Bourbon whiskey was named. Kentucke County by 15 Stars revives the first naming of Kentucky that started it all.

“Bourbon, America and Kentucky all began together,” said Ricky Johnson, co-founder of 15 Stars. “We carry the spirit and craftsmanship of early Kentucky in our bones and express it in every bottle, delivering the aged flavor of whiskeys often priced twice as high.”

OK then!

Kentucke County Bourbon 6 Years Old

Pretty simple: Two Kentucky straight bourbon whiskeys, both with minimum ages of 6 years, are blended into this release. Neither seems overly exciting, the finished product here offering a basic construction that won’t really rock the boat. Aromas of peanut and popcorn dominate, with a punch of clove adding a bold spice to the nose. Brown butter, perhaps a little scorched, adds a savory note, before things turn a touch beefy.

The palate is similarly, well, a bit flat. Doughy overtones of roasted almonds and peanut are downright immersive, ultimately taking the whiskey into somewhat muddy territory. Vanilla notes feel blunt and underdeveloped, the finish coming across as underdeveloped and a bit rustic, layered with elements of hemp rope, wet cigarettes, and horse saddle. Fine as a mixer. Otherwise forgettable. 90 proof. B- / $38

Kentucke County American Whiskey 12 Years Old

Here we have an oddity: A blend of straight bourbon and American whiskey which was distilled from a bourbon mashbill and aged 7 years in second-use oak before an additional 5 years in new charred oak. Distilled in Kentucky and Indiana.

This is a more complex experience from the start, fruitier but also more heavily punctuated with barrel char and a meaty underbelly… but the aromatics don’t tell you the whole story.

While the nose gets increasingly savory as it sits in the glass, the palate meanders its way toward fruit, a blend of strawberry and baked apple melding with sesame paste and dusted with cinnamon. Malted milk, well-torched banana slices dipped in caramel, and flambeed pears add some secondary character, but those expecting anything approaching a 12 year old bourbon experience will come away sorely disappointed, as a flood of peanut butter on the finish wipes away most of the proceedings. I left the experience with a sigh. 90 proof. B / $58

content:
Texas-born bourbons are not exactly known for their delicacy, and Garrison Brothers — which stakes a claim as being “the first corn to cork bourbon distillery in America opened beyond Kentucky, and the first legal whiskey distillery in Texas” — has long stood proudly on those very laurels. While its standard Texas Straight Bourbon and a few other expressions are well known and widely available, Garrison Brothers also has a limited edition bottling called Balmorhea. This special edition has been released only once before; below we look at the second release of the whiskey, which arrives for 2019.

What’s Balmorhea? It’s a West Texas State Park that contains an enormous swimming pool, the largest spring-fed pool in the world. With Balmorhea whiskey, Garrison Brothers donates $5 from every bottle sold to preserving, restoring, and landscaping this park.

So what are you getting? The whiskey in the bottle is not simply repackaged Garrison Brothers Texas Straight Bourbon. Rather, it’s a double-aged bourbon that starts with its standard sweet mashbill, which is then aged for four years in new American white oak barrels made from Ozarks-harvested wood. A second aging involves an extra year in half-size white oak barrels made from trees grown in Minnesota.

Let’s give it a try!

Note: With this updated post, we’re consolidating our Balmorhea coverage to offer a look at the whiskey as it changes over the years.

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2026) Review

We missed the 2025 release, but we’re back for a look at 2026’s offering. The formula hasn’t changed, but a single barrel offering (not reviewed) was released this year in very limited quantities. Balmorhea has never been shy with wood, and 2026’s release is no exception to the rule, though this year’s release sees all that heavy tannin a bit better integrated into the experience. Heavy char slides toward dark chocolate and anise on the nose, then on to coffee — dark roast, just shy of burnt. The palate is more invigorating, though the winey notes of 2024 and earlier are largely absent here. In their stead, the char notes become increasingly smoky, while the coffee notes turn slightly sweet. More effusive notes of chocolate, cinnamon, and a lightly herbal chicory note give the midpalate and beyond a real lift, the finish settling back into some racy cherry notes, edged with fresh green herbs. It’s altogether more of a lip-smacking crowd-pleaser (while still exuding just a touch of that trademark Garrison Bros. funk) — and definitely a step in the right direction. 115 proof. A- / $180 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2024) Review

(Previous editions have used oak from different forests for the two barrels; no word on wood sourcing this year, though.) Unlike Guadalupe (and other Garrison special editions), Balmorhea has year-round availability. Coffee-brown in the glass, this is Garrison Brothers at peak Garrison Brothers, taking everything you know about the brand and amping at up another notch. The nose is dense with wood and char, showcasing coffee bean, oxidized wine, saddle leather, and fresh-cut lumber — all the fixins to survive a cool night at the ranch. The whiskey positively broods in the glass, with layers of cloves and more coffee, barbecue char, and that inimitable, oxidized Madeira quality that I’ve remarked on in prior vintages. Dusky and increasingly herbal as the finish builds, the drinker is left with lingering notes of rosemary, accented by ample notes of mesquite smoke. 115 proof. B+ / $180 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2023) Review

Balmorhea was first released in 2017, and it comes with a commitment from the distillery to donate $5 from each sale to Balmorhea State Park, home of the one of the world’s largest natural spring swimming pools. To date, the distillery has donated more than $78,000 to Texas Parks & Wildlife Foundation. Last reviewed here in 2019, 2023’s version is arrives with the same approach as always: Double barreling that sees the whiskey spend four years in new American white oak barrels made from wood harvested from the Ozarks, then another year in barrels made from Minnesota trees.

Racier than the Small Batch but still firmly represented on the ranch, Balmorhea sees Garrison Brothers taking a more alcohol-driven yet sweeter approach to the house style. It remains boldly spicy with cloves and allspice notes offering an aggressive punch, but the whiskey tempers some of the rye-driven grass and woody barrel influence with welcome elements of mint and basil. The palate feels quite similar, both burly and spicy, with a candied ginger quality emerging with time in glass. Punchy with cloves and dark espresso notes, the whisky finds a sherried, almost Maderized quality after it’s spent a half hour or so in glass, culminating in a finish that mixes together dates, raisins, and walnuts. Definitely a step up from the Small Batch, it’s a curious combination of both Old World and New World styles — all done with American oak from start to finish. 115 proof. A- / $140 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2019) Review

This is an incredibly intense whiskey, the color of (weakish) coffee, impossible to see anything but hazy light through it. The nose cues you in right away to what to expect, with heavy notes of barrel char, coffee bean, and candied pecans. Smoky with mesquite notes, there’s a pungency of black olives and smoldering eucalyptus branches underneath the surface.

On the palate, intensity reigns. An incredible amount of barrel char and campfire smoke notes dominate, though with enough time some sweetness starts to emerge in the form of maple, vanilla, and dark cocoa powder notes. That’s all so well-hidden under a wall of wood that water is all but mandatory here, and said water manages to soften the wood quite a bit, bringing out new notes of cherry and gingerbread spice, cloves and coffee. Bold, pungent, and chewy even with this addition, Balmorhea is about as far from a “starter whiskey” as you can get — though it is often worth the challenge. 115 proof. 6000 bottles produced. B+ / $140  [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

content:
Crescent 9 is one of the longest-lived and best-selling THC beverage brands on the market, with a heavy focus on its canned seltzers. Crescent 9 is unique in the massive range of dosage it packs into its beverages, with the amount of THC included in a can ranging from 5mg to a whopping 50mg. Products are available as solo packs or in mixed cases, all containing the same amount of THC. (5mg THC seltzers also include 4mg CBD; there’s no mention of CBD in the higher dosage cans.)

Today we look at four of Crescent 9’s seltzer flavors, all featuring 5mg or 10mg THC dosage.

Crescent 9 Ginger Lemonade 5mg THC Seltzer – Easily the best product I’ve tasted from Crescent 9, this offers a bright, refreshing ginger punch that compares well with a craft bottle of ginger beer. Lemon plays second fiddle but is certainly detectable, particularly after the fiery ginger settles down a bit. Gently sweet but crafted with restraint, this one goes down way too easy. A

Crescent 9 Ginger Lemonade 10mg THC Seltzer – Not notably different than the 5mg expression, with an equally strong ginger bite and that lingering lemon note adding a sour punch. Just as good, with a stronger THC punch. A

Crescent 9 Tropical 5mg THC Seltzer – Terpenes burst from the can upon cracking it open but soon settle down, the seltzer quickly approximating a a fizzy version of canned Dole pineapple juice. There’s a slightly funky edge visible, perhaps because the seltzer comes across on the watery side, though the moderated acidity and finishing hints of spice help lift it up a bit. B

Crescent 9 Raspberry Lime 5mg THC Seltzer – Again there’s a strong terpene aroma when cracking open a can, though lime is detectable as a secondary aromatic quality. Sipping on the drink reveals an insane amount of fruit — raspberry, candylike — waiting in the wings. It’s helpful at throwing sugar water on some of the terpene character to temper it, but the cloying aftertaste it leaves you with can be daunting. B

Crescent 9 Raspberry Lime 10mg THC Seltzer – An even stronger terpene note dominates this experience, with fruity raspberry aromas more dominant here than in the 5mg version. Things settle down into a long and expectedly sweet conclusion, though the cannabinoid tempering actually helps to tame some of the overtly candylike notes. B

Crescent 9 Sour Watermelon 5mg THC Seltzer – A little sweet, a little sour, and stuffed with the essence of watermelon candy that have melted in the sun. As with many Crescent 9 expressions, this one grows on you as you sit with it for a bit, though that sharp and candylike fruitiness never feels particularly grown-up to sip on. You know exactly what this tastes like before you ever crack open the can. B

Crescent 9 Sour Watermelon 10mg THC Seltzer – No major shifts, though this shows off stronger terpene notes that dull some of the overt hard candy sweetness. There are pros and cons to that, which causes the entire affair to come out roughly even. B

Crescent 9 Grape Lemonade 10mg THC Seltzer – A wildly sweetened approximation of purple drink, the heavily candied attack is somehow abutted by a substantial terpene quality, especially visible on the nose, which manages to go toe to toe with the sugary body. Blunt and lacking in much of anything that would appeal to most grown-ups. C

$70 per 16-pack of 12 oz. cans

content:
I have always maintained that well-aged single grain Scotch is an incredibly underrated category. Single malts tend to get all the attention when it comes to fancy age statements, while grain is usually working in the background, quietly providing the foundation to blends. Give a good grain new make a couple of decades in oak, and with the right cask/s, it can become something truly special.

Today we’re looking at the 1991 vintage from North British Distillery, bottled for Duncan Taylor’s Octave series. Distilled in 1991, and bottled in 2016 at 25 years old, this whisky spent its years in an ex-bourbon cask before resting for a few months in a sherry octave before being bottled at a healthy 51.6% abv. With an outturn of only 60 bottles, this is a relatively niche release for the South African market, released through retailer WhiskyBrother.

North British is one of Scotland’s major grain distilleries, a joint venture between Diageo and Edrington, and it produces spirit mostly destined for blending rather than neat sipping, which makes independent bottlings like this all the more interesting. With 25 years behind it and a finishing cask small enough to have a significant influence on the spirit, this bottlings gives us an opportunity to see what the distillery can do when given center stage.

The Octave North British 25 Years Old 1991 Review

The nose is immediately rich and inviting. There is plenty of dried fruit here, with raisins and cooked fruit sitting alongside vanilla, honey, and a touch of citrus. The sherry cask brings some darker notes into the picture, with chocolate, nuts, and a hint of toasted oak.

Given the age, there is remarkably little sense of tired oak. Instead, this whisky has developed the softer, rounder character you would expect from a quarter-century in wood without losing the gentle sweetness that makes grain whisky so approachable. The octave finish is without a doubt noticeable, but doesn’t completely dominate the spirit or the bourbon cask.

The palate is really where this whisky starts to show its strength. At 51.6% abv, there is plenty of intensity, but it is surprisingly easy to drink. Sweet malt, dried fruit, and chocolate arrive first, followed by vanilla, toasted nuts, and a little spice. The body has a pleasantly oily quality, giving the whisky more weight than you’d expect from a single grain. The sherry influence becomes more apparent as the whisky develops in the glass. Darker fruit and chocolate gradually give way to pepper, oak spice, and a slight nuttiness.

The finish is medium-long, with lingering chocolate, dried fruit, oak spice, and a touch of sweetness. It doesn’t have an enormous complexity like well-aged malts, but that isn’t really the point. What this does offer is balance, character, and a rather convincing argument for paying more attention to mature grain whisky.

For me, this bottle is a great example of why I love independent releases: It takes a relatively anonymous component of the scotch industry and gives it an opportunity to stand on its own. Twenty five years of maturation and a well-chosen sherry octave have transformed what is often used for blending into a liquid absolutely worth enjoying on its own.

103.2 proof.

A / $205

content:
There’s no shortage of IPAs at Seattle’s Elysian, so it may be easy to dismiss Jacktail Hazy IPA as just another member of a very large crowd. But Elysian doesn’t product a lot of hazy IPAs, with Contact Haze its most notable offering. At 6.1% IPA this has a similar heft, though a much different vibe. The overt tropical notes of Contact Haze are here, replaced with a more mellow tropical character, more of a fresh pineapple note, followed by hints of vanilla and a lighter red fruit character, almost strawberry — then banana. The general restraint on alcohol helps make this more crushable than it should be, giving its depth of flavor.

6.1% abv.

A- / $14 per six-pack

content:
After our time in Bordeaux, team Drinkhacker headed south to Spain and its coastal Basque Country, posting up in the delightful town of San Sebastian. Pintxos culture couldn’t be more fun — standing in crowded bars, sipping on local txakoli wine, and chowing down on one bar snack after another. Used napkins? Tossed on the floor! It’s a lifestyle that doesn’t seem particularly healthy — rarely dining before 10pm, rarely consuming anything resembling a vegetable — but one which I could (and did) easily get used to.

From here it’s about an hour and a half to Rioja, another iconic wine region but one which is dramatically different than Bordeaux. (Along with Priorat, Rioja is one of only two DOCs in Spain.) Here, mountains hem in a sprawling, hilly valley that is absolutely covered with vines, a stark contrast to the tiny, often flat vineyards of France. The landscape is decidedly reminiscent of California, albeit even hotter.

Abutting the laconic Ebro River, wineries here measure their production in the hundreds of thousands of bottles each year, their cellars stretching seemingly forever with barrel after barrel of (mostly) tempranillo, along with smaller quantities of graciano, garnacha, maturana, and wines made from other heritage varietals. Rioja spans three regions: Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa, and Rioja Oreintal. All of the wineries except one that we visited were based in Rioja Alta — though many have vineyards across all three regions.

On this leg of the trip, we made our base in the town of Lagrono, which has its own pintxos scene to enjoy in the evening after a day of making the rounds to the bodegas of the region.

Unlike Bordeaux, the wineries of Rioja were very accommodating to media visits, and setting up appointments was not particularly difficult. (Thanks to the Consorzio Regulador DOCa Rioja for helping us make arrangements.) We visited a total of five spots, and I’ll tell you all about them in the writeups below.

Finca Valpiedra

Finca Valpiedra, like many wineries in Rioja, operates multiple facilities and labels, including Bujanda and Montepedroso. Tours and tastings are at the Valpiedra location, however. Our guide Paola loaded us into a Jeep to tour the terraced vineyards here, which stretch all the way down to the river’s waterfront. The massive stones that dominate the floors of the vineyard make the rocky soils of Bordeaux look like tiny pebbles. And as in Bordeaux, blazing temperatures forced the earliest harvest ever here, and harvest was well underway during our visit.

One of the most interesting parts of this vineyard tour was a close look at the Spanish practice of overgrafting, where a young vine is grafted not onto young rootstock but onto an older, healthy vine, Frankenstein-like. It’s a curious but apparently successful way to deal with the increasingly hot climate, which is hostile to young vines, while helping get the new vine to maturity much faster. It also looks slightly crazy.

We sampled three wines here — paired with local cheese and charcuterie, almost ubiquitous when tasting in the region — with a deeper dive into two Rioja offerings, a young 2022 Cantos de Valpiedra and a more mature 2018 Finca Valpiedra Reserva. This was an excellent way to get a fresh grounding on how the young joven style (very fruity with light florals) and the richer, older Reservas differ when placed side by side. The dense minerality of the Reserva was particularly bright in today’s tasting.

El Montecillo, s/n, 26360 Fuenmayor, La Rioja

Bodegas Marques de Riscal

This is probably the most visited and definitely the most photographed winery in Rioja, and it isn’t because of the wine. It’s because of a structure erected here 20 years ago that was designed by Frank Gehry. Turns out this isn’t part of the winery at all but rather a 61-room hotel, operated by Marriott. It’s quite breathtaking to behold but is certainly starting to show its age inside; the corridors particularly could use some freshening up considering the exorbitant price of staying here (typically $1000 a night and up).

The adjacent winery finds us across the Ebro in the Rioja Alavesa region, and it hosts a robust tour operation, complete with buses dropping off large groups of people who go on packed tours of a facility that turns out 10 million bottles per year. Despite the relatively impersonal nature of the tour here, it was still worthwhile and featured tastes of three wines — my favorite being a white Rueda with its green apple and gentle tropical notes. After the tour, our host offered samples of Riscal‘s 2022 Reserva XR, a special version of its Reserva designed to be softer and better balanced. Made from Riscal’s oldest vines, it’s a chewy, chocolate-heavy wine that is mostly sold in restaurants. As promised, I felt it offered a much more nuanced version of what Rioja has to offer, and was a top taste for the winery. (While not offered on the tour, you can buy a glass in the cafe.)

Calle Torrea, 1, 01340 Elciego, Araba

Bodegas Muga

Day two found us traveling to the Rioja Alta town of Haro, where some of Rioja’s best-known wineries can be found in a concentrated cluster together, all within walking distance of one another. We had a bit of a rocky start here, as our reservation had been misplaced, but after righting the situation enjoyed a lengthy and informative tour of the facility, complete with a look at its own cooperage; this is one of the only wineries in the country that produces its own vats and barrels.

Fun fact: In Spain, Muga markets its Reserva as a younger Crianza. Why? In the local market, older wines are generally shunned for fear they will be overly woody. It’s the same wine, but with a younger designation on the label, it sells better.

The typical tasting here includes just two wines, a white Rioja and Muga’s Selection Especial Reserva, but we were treated to a tasting of almost everything in the tasting room after the official tour wrapped.

This deep dive into eight additional varieties was one of the most instructive experiences I had on the trip, and I really fell in love with Muga’s 2019 Prado Enea Gran Reserva, a wildly distinctive wine with notes of licorice, slate, and nutmeg all on display atop an almost Port-like fruitiness (though sans the sweetness). Even the comparatively young 2021 Torre Muga was approachable despite its significant density; our guide Carmen suggested it would be much more refined in just six more months.

Avenida Vizcaya, Barrio de la Estación, 2, 26200 Haro, La Rioja

Bodegas La Rioja Alta

We hopped into this tasting room around the corner from Muga without an appointment because our guide suggested La Rioja Alta Gran Reserva 904 would be a fun comparison against Prado Enea. We bought a glass of the 2016 release (plus an albarino from a sister winery in Rias Baixas) and found the similarities intriguing. Lots of cocoa, currants, and some mint. A little less Port-like than Prado Enea, but quite a soulful wine to sample. Lovely grounds here, and I would have enjoyed a deeper dive into the place.

Avenida Vizcaya, 8, 26200 Haro, La Rioja

Mystery Winery

I hate to do this to you, but our final stop was at one of Rioja’s most internet-famous producers, and if you spend any time on Reddit’s r/wine boards you’ll know immediately who I’m talking about. The winery is open to visits and tastings only to media and industry professionals, and we were offered a tour on the condition that I do not write about it or post anything about the place on social media. That was a first for me, but I agreed, so I’ll leave it mostly at that. It was quite a wild tour, complete with a descent into its 150-year old cellars (pictured above) and a tasting of two of its well-aged Reservas. (2014 and 2015 are the current vintages!)

If you do figure out who I’m talking about, know that you can visit the winery’s small shop and purchase a bottle of wine (including half bottles) to take home or sip on site. Good luck!

With Crane Cove Rye Whiskey, part of the 2026 Distillery Series, the company ventured into…

The post Review: Brucato Spirits Crane Cove Rye appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Most sourced whiskey travels a long way before it reaches the bottle. Crane Cove Rye takes a rather different route.

Brucato Spirits is a small, independent spirits company based in San Francisco’s Mission District, best known for its California-inspired amaro. With Crane Cove Rye Whiskey, part of the 2026 Distillery Series, the company ventured into whiskey while keeping its sourcing remarkably close to home. Rather than bringing in barrels from Indiana or Kentucky, Brucato sourced this whiskey from Anchor Distilling in San Francisco’s Potrero Hill neighborhood. In other words, this may be a sourced whiskey, but it is very much a San Francisco whiskey.

There is another detail that makes Crane Cove Rye stand apart: the mashbill is 100% malted rye. The grain, sourced from Briess Malting in Wisconsin and grown in the upper Midwest, underwent a two-day upward step fermentation using Anchor Brewing’s ale yeast. The fermentation produced considerable foam and a wort around 9% ABV. Anchor also left the spent grain with the liquid during distillation rather than separating the two beforehand.

The resulting distillate went through double copper pot distillation on a 1,500-liter wash still and a 700-liter spirit still fitted with an agitator. On January 13, 2017, the distillate entered two 53-gallon Cooper’s Reserve barrels at 123.9 proof. Those barrels were eventually dumped in the second half of June 2026, giving the whiskey nine years and five months of maturation.

The barrels themselves were no ordinary containers. Made by Independent Stave Company from fine-grain American white oak, they were open-air seasoned for 24 months, given a #3 char over an oak scrap fire, and subjected to a heavy toast. The Cooper’s Reserve barrels cost roughly four times as much as a standard distillery barrel. After the two barrels were blended, the whiskey came out at its natural harvest proof of 129.

For a small San Francisco spirits company, there is plenty here to set Crane Cove Rye apart from the usual sourced-whiskey story: local distillation, 100% malted rye, ale yeast fermentation, copper pot distillation, nearly a decade in Cooper’s Reserve barrels, and a final proof of 129.

Is this unusual San Francisco rye whiskey worthy of attention beyond the confines of Bay Area locals? Let’s find out.

Brucato Spirits Crane Cove Rye 9 Years Old Review

The nose starts with plenty of juicy, ripe fruit, led by freshly sliced cantaloupe and white grape juice. As the fruit settles, honey graham crackers bring a sweet, bready aroma alongside milk chocolate. For those encountering malted rye for the first time, it is worth comparing it with the much more common unmalted rye whiskey that remains the industry standard. The malting process tends to yield rye whiskey that is soft, fruity, and floral, and all three qualities are readily apparent on the nose.

The palate starts with less-sweet wild blackberries before moving into pine needles. The mid-palate turns spicy with clove, followed by a familiar dill note and a very dense mouthfeel. The finish moves toward a more traditional rye profile, with white pepper joining stewed green apple, followed by another push of clove and a final touch of cocoa powder.

Overall, this is a beautiful example of malted rye whiskey. I tend to gravitate toward rye whiskey in general, in large part because of the diversity the category offers, and malted rye remains an underrepresented style within the category. This is the longest-aged malted rye I have experienced, and I am very pleased with the result. Even after nine years in new charred oak barrels, the fruity qualities of the malted rye grain remain clearly present.

110 proof.

B+ / $99

title: Review: Woodford Reserve Master’s Collection Super Seasoned Oak Bourbon

Super Seasoned Oak has nothing to do with spice or pepper but rather refers to the practice of “seasoning” newly milled barrel staves by letting them dry in…

The post Review: Woodford Reserve Master’s Collection Super Seasoned Oak Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Woodford Reserve‘s 22nd installment of its beloved Master’s Collection is upon us, and while these experimental releases can be out-there, this 2026 expression is something quite unusual. Super Seasoned Oak has nothing to do with spice or pepper but rather refers to the practice of “seasoning” newly milled barrel staves by letting them dry in the open air before they are used to create casks. (The process reduces harsh tannins and allows tight wood grain to open up, allowing liquid to seep into it.) Traditional oak staves must be seasoned for a year or two before they are put to use in barrel construction. With Super Seasoned Oak, those staves spend between five and seven years drying before being turned into barrels.

Surprisingly, there’s no additional information about the actual whiskey that was aged in these barrels, but it’s safe to say it’s the standard Woodford bourbon recipe, aged for roughly the same amount of time as the standby.

Woodford Reserve Master’s Collection Super Seasoned Oak Bourbon Review

The results here are solid, and quite surprising. While I would suspect there are diminishing returns to be gained after the first few years of leaving wood outside to dry, it turns out the excessive drying time coaxes out plenty of sugar from the wood… which ends up in the whiskey.

The nose is at first familiar (though not wholly Woodfordian), with an ample, peanutty sweetness that hits heavy from the start. Vanilla is dominant, with notes of maple adding even more sweetness to the aroma. Fruit picks up from there (primarily raisin), but it can be a little slow going, with a traditional barrel char note lingering over the proceedings. All told, that sweet vanilla-driven syrupiness makes for a decidedly dessert-like attack that sets the stage for the experience to come.

The palate does not let off the gas. This is a very sweet whiskey, that peanut character emerging as candied brittle, laced more clearly with maple and some raisin notes. Heavy cinnamon notes build significantly, layering with tons of vanilla to create a creamy flavor that would be perfectly at home as a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream flavor. The spicy richness clings to every corner of the mouth, layers of increasingly dark, dried berries dripping over the top of the bourbon. A raisin/prune character lingers on the finish, injected heavily with baking spice and, as it sits in glass, a bit of hoary creosote that sees some tannic funk creeping in.

To be frank, I was not expecting this level of sweetness from the whiskey — particularly given that it’s a Woodford product — and ultimately I found it a bit much to handle. While it’s very instructive in showcasing what excessive wood seasoning can do to a whiskey, it’s not particularly balanced, making it more useful as a proof of concept rather than a full-scale sipper.

100.4 proof.

B+ / $180

title: Review: Dark Arts Sherry Garcia Bourbon Vol. 3
summary:

They track releases, compare batches, trade bottles, swap information and know exactly which distillery produced what, where a particular barrel came from and when the next release is expected. Give them a scarce bottle from a whiskey maker…

The post Review: Dark Arts Sherry Garcia Bourbon Vol. 3 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
There is a certain kind of bourbon drinker who does not simply buy whiskey. They follow it. They track releases, compare batches, trade bottles, swap information and know exactly which distillery produced what, where a particular barrel came from and when the next release is expected. Give them a scarce bottle from a whiskey maker they trust, and they will go looking for it.

That kind of devotion should sound familiar to anyone who has spent time around Grateful Dead fans.

Deadheads built a culture around following the band, collecting recordings, trading information and showing up again and again, sometimes traveling considerable distances to be part of the experience. The music was certainly at the center of it, but the community surrounding the band became its own phenomenon. For many fans, being a Deadhead was about far more than owning a few albums. It was about participation.

There is a similar spirit among the followers of Dark Arts Whiskey House. The bourbon world has no shortage of whiskey, but Dark Arts has managed to build its own devoted following, one release at a time. Its bottles have become objects of pursuit for drinkers who pay attention to what the whiskey house is doing and are eager to see what comes next.

Which brings us to a bottle with a name that could hardly be more appropriate for this particular comparison.

In the fall of 2026, Dark Arts Whiskey House released Volume 3 of Sherry Garcia Bourbon. Jerry Garcia’s name does not appear on the bottle, but “Sherry Garcia” is close enough to make the joke immediately apparent. The name works because the bourbon has been finished in Oloroso sherry casks, giving Dark Arts a reason to turn a whiskey release into a playful nod to the Grateful Dead’s legendary guitarist.

And perhaps that is where the comparison between Deadheads and bourbon obsessives gets particularly interesting. Both groups have spent years proving that following something can be as important as simply possessing it. There is always another show, another recording, another bottle, another release. You can chase it, study it, talk about it and argue about it with people who are just as invested as you are.

Volume 3 starts with bourbon distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, from a mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye and 4% malted barley. The label states that the bourbon is at least 8.5 years old, though the blend ranges from bourbon aged for 8 years and 9 months to bourbon aged for 9 years and 10 months.

That bourbon then underwent secondary maturation in 22 Oloroso sherry casks, each holding 59 gallons. The Oloroso casks were filled over a period stretching from November 2024 through March 2026.

Dark Arts’ latest release sits at the intersection of two particularly devoted tribes. One follows whiskey. The other follows Jerry Garcia and the Grateful Dead. Both know a thing or two about chasing the next thing down the road.

Is Volume 3 of Sherry Garcia something for which the bourbon community can be grateful?

Or is it dead on arrival?

Let’s find out.

Dark Arts Sherry Garcia Bourbon Vol. 3 (2026) Review

The nose opens with dried cranberries, and very dry ones at that, with little of their original moisture remaining. The cranberry note is prominent, more akin to the dusty aroma of fully dried fruit, followed by dense chocolate fudge that brings plenty of creaminess. As the bourbon opens in the glass, charred orange peel and very dark caramel begin to show.

The overall nose is exceptionally well integrated. The Oloroso sherry never becomes overwhelming, while the chocolate avoids veering into excessive tannin.

The palate brings plenty of red fruit, but in a much brighter form: maraschino cherry syrup. It is an unusually bright, sweet cherry note given the dark dried cherry profile found on the nose. Orange peel joins the cherry, followed by roasted hazelnuts and milk chocolate through the mid-palate. Taken together, those flavors present something remarkably close to the composite profile of Nutella, all wrapped in a very dense mouthfeel.

The finish brings the bourbon back toward the profile established on the nose, with dried cherry joining dark chocolate. The chocolate is less sweet here than the fudge presented on the nose, while clove adds a healthy dose of spice. Toasted pecans bring another layer of oak influence to the finish.

This is easily one of the more enjoyable Oloroso sherry finishes I have experienced, with impressive consistency from the first aroma through the final sip. For anyone looking for a top-notch example of an Oloroso sherry-finished bourbon, this is it.

114.06 proof.

A / $100

title: Review: Wines of San Felice, 2026 Releases
summary:
San Felice is one of our favorite Italian wine producers, the brand creating a wide range of wines from throughout Tuscany — though primarily Chianti Classico. The post Review: Wines of San Felice, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
San Felice is one of our favorite Italian wine producers, the brand creating a wide range of wines from throughout Tuscany — though primarily Chianti Classico.

Today we look at five 2026 releases from the producer, all excellent and well worth your while.

2024 San Felice In Avane Chardonnay Toscana IGT – A new wine to me, this is a rather brooding expression of chardonnay. The restrained offering finds itself a bit bitter on the attack, notes of lime leaf tucking in to underripe apple, white florals, and lemon curd as the palate develops. The expected breakthrough into more exuberant fruitiness along with some salinity on the finish never really arrives, the affair stopping short before it feels like things really get going. Flashes of interest, however. B+ / $40

2023 San Felice Borgo Chianti Classico DOCG – Iconic Chianti, this offers a bright, cherry-fueled attack that is laced through and through with green herbs, hints of anise, and some dark chocolate. Ample acidity keeps the wine lively and refreshing, with citrusy notes developing as the finish approaches. There’s lemon and orange peel here, evoking thoughts of mostarda and cut grass. Quite versatile and lovely throughout. A- / $40

2022 San Felice Pugnitello Toscana IGT – Punchy and driven by tobacco and dark chocolate notes, San Felice (which is one of the premiere developers of pugnitello) has refined this grape to showcase its more savory characteristics — heavy on licorice, tobacco, light touches of tar — while simultaneously allowing fruit to peek through the cracks. Black cherry, blackberry, and late-game rhubarb all offer a juicy but almost wintry quality to the wine, though intense acidity and more moderated tannins keep everything both tight and lively. I’d hold this for a few years just to see what happens. A- / $95

2022 San Felice Il Grigio Chianti Classico Riserva DOCG – Surprisingly more fruit-forward than expected for a Riserva level Chianti Classico, this unabashedly cherry-fueled offers gentle tertiary notes of cloves and a touch of black tea, before a brighter raspberry-fueled finish comes into focus. Any licorice notes on the finish are more candied, fitting in perfectly with the theme to date. A- / $37

2021 San Felice Campogiovanni Brunello di Montalcino DOCG – A thick and slightly raisiny wine with chocolate overtones, this Brunello leans richer than is typical, its cherry and wild berry notes comparatively muted. Dark caramel and even more chocolate notes build from there, leading to a gravelly charcoal and toasty anise conclusion. The overtly oxidized sweetness, almost date-lake, becomes thick on the finish, finding a foil in a heavy layer of vanilla. The palate ends up all but coated with the extracted, almost jammy character. A bit too heavy for me. B+ / $84

2022 San Felice La Pieve Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG – As with Borgo, this presents a classic Chianti structure — tightly wound cherry, layered tannins, and modest spice to even it all out. The anise is lightened up, which lets the chocolate character fire more freely, notes of graphite and turned earth both becoming prominent as the finish emerges. For all its depth of flavor, the wine is surprisingly straightforward, never deviating from its mission, though the cherry turns more toward blackberry on the lengthy, exuberant, and wholly enjoyable finish. Sometimes, a seamless through-line works out just fine. A / $95

The post Review: New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
New Riff Distillery hasn’t been slowing down one bit. They recently completed a significant expansion at their Newport, Kentucky distillery, increasing production capacity by 50%, and they’ve added the necessary barrel warehousing at a nearby site. They also increased their distribution footprint to include whiskey-hungry Florida and Illinois. And they remain, as ever, dedicated to making what they call “whiskey riffs.” The latest, however, is actually a riff on a riff. I’ll let them explain:

“Last year we released our Malted Rye Whiskey, and experiencing its remarkably elegant, sophisticated character gave us another idea,” said co-founder Jay Erisman. “We think of it as a malt whiskey first and a rye whiskey second, which raised the question: what would happen if we treated it like other malt whiskies and aged it in sherry casks?”

New Riff’s first batches of 100% Malted Rye Whiskey were distilled in 2014, and the initial release landed in May 2021. For this sherry finished elaboration, New Riff imported custom-made 53-gallon Spanish sherry casks and filled them with 5-year-old New Riff Malted Rye Whiskey. Twelve oloroso and three Pedro Ximenez casks were filled with whiskey and aged another year, before being vatted in the fall of 2021 and left to marry and condition together for several following months until they were bottled in spring of 2022 (at cask strength).

The distillery has put out no shortage of winning “riffs” in recent years, including the malted rye at the heart of this expression. Let’s see how the latest edition stacks up.

Update: We’re adding fresh coverage of this re-released whiskey to expand this review.

New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (2022) Review

The sherry finishing and higher proof have definitely added some heft to the aroma compared to the standard malted rye with ample spice cabinet and leathery notes of dark berries and sweet almond paste. The sherry isn’t overpowering though, and things remain fairly wood-driven with cinnamon stick and toasty barrel char growing more prominent as it opens in the glass. The palate showcases even more sweet sherry character with bold, syrupy notes of blackberry cobbler and raspberry candies. The rye spice is unusually a bit more prominent than in the original, with black pepper and clove popping on the mid-palate and segueing to a generous finish of cooked red fruits, some mild oaky astringency, and lingering notes of tobacco and cherry juice.

Like past limited editions, this bottle was made available only to New Riff’s Whiskey Club and select retailers. However, the success of Malted Rye last year has landed it in the New Riff core lineup, so perhaps we will be seeing even more of this sherry-finished expression in the future. 112.7 proof. A- / $65 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (2026) Review

A few small changes: The previous release started with 5-year-old malted rye and this year’s whiskey started as 6-year-old malted rye. Both were finished in oloroso and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks. Both hit the bottle at cask strength but this year’s release is 2.5% stronger.

The nose of this reissued offering is big and sings both rye and sherry notes at full volume. Raisin and cinnamon sticks hit first, wrapped in leather. Raspberry compote comes next along with caramel and some clove. A touch of cereal grain follows through at the end.

Sipped neat, the whiskey hits hard. In his review four years ago, Drew noted that the rye spices are bolder in this finished whiskey than they are in the unfinished rye, and that is absolutely still the case in the newest release. Sharp cinnamon, fresh cracked black pepper, and clove come bursting out of the glass along with an alcohol bite. Immediately following come sherry notes including raspberry preserves, blackberry, and caramel. Midpalate brings some vanilla to the mix, which stays through the long finish. The good folks at New Riff recommend adding water to bring out the sherry notes or abstaining to highlight the rye. I gave both a try, and it’s true, but the rye notes never disappeared with the addition of water.

Altogether, this a well crafted whiskey that deserves serious attention from fans of both rye whiskey and sherry-finished single malts. -RL 117.3 proof. A- / $70

The post Review: Kentucke County Bourbon 6 Years Old and American Whiskey 12 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Not a typo. “Kentucke County,” with an “e,” is the name of the product. It’s a new sub-label from 15 Stars, which has been spinning off other “Kentucky heritage” brands like First West of late, with two expressions available at launch. (“Both in commemorative, collectible bottles,” presumably because of the “250th anniversary” sticker below the front label.)

What’s this Kentucke all about?

In 1776, the same year the American colonies declared their independence, Kentucke County was established as Virginia’s western frontier county. The region would later evolve into the Kentucke District, within which Bourbon County was created, and Bourbon whiskey was named. Kentucke County by 15 Stars revives the first naming of Kentucky that started it all.

“Bourbon, America and Kentucky all began together,” said Ricky Johnson, co-founder of 15 Stars. “We carry the spirit and craftsmanship of early Kentucky in our bones and express it in every bottle, delivering the aged flavor of whiskeys often priced twice as high.”

OK then!

Kentucke County Bourbon 6 Years Old

Pretty simple: Two Kentucky straight bourbon whiskeys, both with minimum ages of 6 years, are blended into this release. Neither seems overly exciting, the finished product here offering a basic construction that won’t really rock the boat. Aromas of peanut and popcorn dominate, with a punch of clove adding a bold spice to the nose. Brown butter, perhaps a little scorched, adds a savory note, before things turn a touch beefy.

The palate is similarly, well, a bit flat. Doughy overtones of roasted almonds and peanut are downright immersive, ultimately taking the whiskey into somewhat muddy territory. Vanilla notes feel blunt and underdeveloped, the finish coming across as underdeveloped and a bit rustic, layered with elements of hemp rope, wet cigarettes, and horse saddle. Fine as a mixer. Otherwise forgettable. 90 proof. B- / $38

Kentucke County American Whiskey 12 Years Old

Here we have an oddity: A blend of straight bourbon and American whiskey which was distilled from a bourbon mashbill and aged 7 years in second-use oak before an additional 5 years in new charred oak. Distilled in Kentucky and Indiana.

This is a more complex experience from the start, fruitier but also more heavily punctuated with barrel char and a meaty underbelly… but the aromatics don’t tell you the whole story.

While the nose gets increasingly savory as it sits in the glass, the palate meanders its way toward fruit, a blend of strawberry and baked apple melding with sesame paste and dusted with cinnamon. Malted milk, well-torched banana slices dipped in caramel, and flambeed pears add some secondary character, but those expecting anything approaching a 12 year old bourbon experience will come away sorely disappointed, as a flood of peanut butter on the finish wipes away most of the proceedings. I left the experience with a sigh. 90 proof. B / $58

content:
Texas-born bourbons are not exactly known for their delicacy, and Garrison Brothers — which stakes a claim as being “the first corn to cork bourbon distillery in America opened beyond Kentucky, and the first legal whiskey distillery in Texas” — has long stood proudly on those very laurels. While its standard Texas Straight Bourbon and a few other expressions are well known and widely available, Garrison Brothers also has a limited edition bottling called Balmorhea. This special edition has been released only once before; below we look at the second release of the whiskey, which arrives for 2019.

What’s Balmorhea? It’s a West Texas State Park that contains an enormous swimming pool, the largest spring-fed pool in the world. With Balmorhea whiskey, Garrison Brothers donates $5 from every bottle sold to preserving, restoring, and landscaping this park.

So what are you getting? The whiskey in the bottle is not simply repackaged Garrison Brothers Texas Straight Bourbon. Rather, it’s a double-aged bourbon that starts with its standard sweet mashbill, which is then aged for four years in new American white oak barrels made from Ozarks-harvested wood. A second aging involves an extra year in half-size white oak barrels made from trees grown in Minnesota.

Let’s give it a try!

Note: With this updated post, we’re consolidating our Balmorhea coverage to offer a look at the whiskey as it changes over the years.

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2026) Review

We missed the 2025 release, but we’re back for a look at 2026’s offering. The formula hasn’t changed, but a single barrel offering (not reviewed) was released this year in very limited quantities. Balmorhea has never been shy with wood, and 2026’s release is no exception to the rule, though this year’s release sees all that heavy tannin a bit better integrated into the experience. Heavy char slides toward dark chocolate and anise on the nose, then on to coffee — dark roast, just shy of burnt. The palate is more invigorating, though the winey notes of 2024 and earlier are largely absent here. In their stead, the char notes become increasingly smoky, while the coffee notes turn slightly sweet. More effusive notes of chocolate, cinnamon, and a lightly herbal chicory note give the midpalate and beyond a real lift, the finish settling back into some racy cherry notes, edged with fresh green herbs. It’s altogether more of a lip-smacking crowd-pleaser (while still exuding just a touch of that trademark Garrison Bros. funk) — and definitely a step in the right direction. 115 proof. A- / $180 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2024) Review

(Previous editions have used oak from different forests for the two barrels; no word on wood sourcing this year, though.) Unlike Guadalupe (and other Garrison special editions), Balmorhea has year-round availability. Coffee-brown in the glass, this is Garrison Brothers at peak Garrison Brothers, taking everything you know about the brand and amping at up another notch. The nose is dense with wood and char, showcasing coffee bean, oxidized wine, saddle leather, and fresh-cut lumber — all the fixins to survive a cool night at the ranch. The whiskey positively broods in the glass, with layers of cloves and more coffee, barbecue char, and that inimitable, oxidized Madeira quality that I’ve remarked on in prior vintages. Dusky and increasingly herbal as the finish builds, the drinker is left with lingering notes of rosemary, accented by ample notes of mesquite smoke. 115 proof. B+ / $180 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2023) Review

Balmorhea was first released in 2017, and it comes with a commitment from the distillery to donate $5 from each sale to Balmorhea State Park, home of the one of the world’s largest natural spring swimming pools. To date, the distillery has donated more than $78,000 to Texas Parks & Wildlife Foundation. Last reviewed here in 2019, 2023’s version is arrives with the same approach as always: Double barreling that sees the whiskey spend four years in new American white oak barrels made from wood harvested from the Ozarks, then another year in barrels made from Minnesota trees.

Racier than the Small Batch but still firmly represented on the ranch, Balmorhea sees Garrison Brothers taking a more alcohol-driven yet sweeter approach to the house style. It remains boldly spicy with cloves and allspice notes offering an aggressive punch, but the whiskey tempers some of the rye-driven grass and woody barrel influence with welcome elements of mint and basil. The palate feels quite similar, both burly and spicy, with a candied ginger quality emerging with time in glass. Punchy with cloves and dark espresso notes, the whisky finds a sherried, almost Maderized quality after it’s spent a half hour or so in glass, culminating in a finish that mixes together dates, raisins, and walnuts. Definitely a step up from the Small Batch, it’s a curious combination of both Old World and New World styles — all done with American oak from start to finish. 115 proof. A- / $140 [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Garrison Brothers Balmorhea Bourbon (2019) Review

This is an incredibly intense whiskey, the color of (weakish) coffee, impossible to see anything but hazy light through it. The nose cues you in right away to what to expect, with heavy notes of barrel char, coffee bean, and candied pecans. Smoky with mesquite notes, there’s a pungency of black olives and smoldering eucalyptus branches underneath the surface.

On the palate, intensity reigns. An incredible amount of barrel char and campfire smoke notes dominate, though with enough time some sweetness starts to emerge in the form of maple, vanilla, and dark cocoa powder notes. That’s all so well-hidden under a wall of wood that water is all but mandatory here, and said water manages to soften the wood quite a bit, bringing out new notes of cherry and gingerbread spice, cloves and coffee. Bold, pungent, and chewy even with this addition, Balmorhea is about as far from a “starter whiskey” as you can get — though it is often worth the challenge. 115 proof. 6000 bottles produced. B+ / $140  [BUY IT NOW FROM RESERVEBAR] [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

content:
Crescent 9 is one of the longest-lived and best-selling THC beverage brands on the market, with a heavy focus on its canned seltzers. Crescent 9 is unique in the massive range of dosage it packs into its beverages, with the amount of THC included in a can ranging from 5mg to a whopping 50mg. Products are available as solo packs or in mixed cases, all containing the same amount of THC. (5mg THC seltzers also include 4mg CBD; there’s no mention of CBD in the higher dosage cans.)

Today we look at four of Crescent 9’s seltzer flavors, all featuring 5mg or 10mg THC dosage.

Crescent 9 Ginger Lemonade 5mg THC Seltzer – Easily the best product I’ve tasted from Crescent 9, this offers a bright, refreshing ginger punch that compares well with a craft bottle of ginger beer. Lemon plays second fiddle but is certainly detectable, particularly after the fiery ginger settles down a bit. Gently sweet but crafted with restraint, this one goes down way too easy. A

Crescent 9 Ginger Lemonade 10mg THC Seltzer – Not notably different than the 5mg expression, with an equally strong ginger bite and that lingering lemon note adding a sour punch. Just as good, with a stronger THC punch. A

Crescent 9 Tropical 5mg THC Seltzer – Terpenes burst from the can upon cracking it open but soon settle down, the seltzer quickly approximating a a fizzy version of canned Dole pineapple juice. There’s a slightly funky edge visible, perhaps because the seltzer comes across on the watery side, though the moderated acidity and finishing hints of spice help lift it up a bit. B

Crescent 9 Raspberry Lime 5mg THC Seltzer – Again there’s a strong terpene aroma when cracking open a can, though lime is detectable as a secondary aromatic quality. Sipping on the drink reveals an insane amount of fruit — raspberry, candylike — waiting in the wings. It’s helpful at throwing sugar water on some of the terpene character to temper it, but the cloying aftertaste it leaves you with can be daunting. B

Crescent 9 Raspberry Lime 10mg THC Seltzer – An even stronger terpene note dominates this experience, with fruity raspberry aromas more dominant here than in the 5mg version. Things settle down into a long and expectedly sweet conclusion, though the cannabinoid tempering actually helps to tame some of the overtly candylike notes. B

Crescent 9 Sour Watermelon 5mg THC Seltzer – A little sweet, a little sour, and stuffed with the essence of watermelon candy that have melted in the sun. As with many Crescent 9 expressions, this one grows on you as you sit with it for a bit, though that sharp and candylike fruitiness never feels particularly grown-up to sip on. You know exactly what this tastes like before you ever crack open the can. B

Crescent 9 Sour Watermelon 10mg THC Seltzer – No major shifts, though this shows off stronger terpene notes that dull some of the overt hard candy sweetness. There are pros and cons to that, which causes the entire affair to come out roughly even. B

Crescent 9 Grape Lemonade 10mg THC Seltzer – A wildly sweetened approximation of purple drink, the heavily candied attack is somehow abutted by a substantial terpene quality, especially visible on the nose, which manages to go toe to toe with the sugary body. Blunt and lacking in much of anything that would appeal to most grown-ups. C

$70 per 16-pack of 12 oz. cans

content:
I have always maintained that well-aged single grain Scotch is an incredibly underrated category. Single malts tend to get all the attention when it comes to fancy age statements, while grain is usually working in the background, quietly providing the foundation to blends. Give a good grain new make a couple of decades in oak, and with the right cask/s, it can become something truly special.

Today we’re looking at the 1991 vintage from North British Distillery, bottled for Duncan Taylor’s Octave series. Distilled in 1991, and bottled in 2016 at 25 years old, this whisky spent its years in an ex-bourbon cask before resting for a few months in a sherry octave before being bottled at a healthy 51.6% abv. With an outturn of only 60 bottles, this is a relatively niche release for the South African market, released through retailer WhiskyBrother.

North British is one of Scotland’s major grain distilleries, a joint venture between Diageo and Edrington, and it produces spirit mostly destined for blending rather than neat sipping, which makes independent bottlings like this all the more interesting. With 25 years behind it and a finishing cask small enough to have a significant influence on the spirit, this bottlings gives us an opportunity to see what the distillery can do when given center stage.

The Octave North British 25 Years Old 1991 Review

The nose is immediately rich and inviting. There is plenty of dried fruit here, with raisins and cooked fruit sitting alongside vanilla, honey, and a touch of citrus. The sherry cask brings some darker notes into the picture, with chocolate, nuts, and a hint of toasted oak.

Given the age, there is remarkably little sense of tired oak. Instead, this whisky has developed the softer, rounder character you would expect from a quarter-century in wood without losing the gentle sweetness that makes grain whisky so approachable. The octave finish is without a doubt noticeable, but doesn’t completely dominate the spirit or the bourbon cask.

The palate is really where this whisky starts to show its strength. At 51.6% abv, there is plenty of intensity, but it is surprisingly easy to drink. Sweet malt, dried fruit, and chocolate arrive first, followed by vanilla, toasted nuts, and a little spice. The body has a pleasantly oily quality, giving the whisky more weight than you’d expect from a single grain. The sherry influence becomes more apparent as the whisky develops in the glass. Darker fruit and chocolate gradually give way to pepper, oak spice, and a slight nuttiness.

The finish is medium-long, with lingering chocolate, dried fruit, oak spice, and a touch of sweetness. It doesn’t have an enormous complexity like well-aged malts, but that isn’t really the point. What this does offer is balance, character, and a rather convincing argument for paying more attention to mature grain whisky.

For me, this bottle is a great example of why I love independent releases: It takes a relatively anonymous component of the scotch industry and gives it an opportunity to stand on its own. Twenty five years of maturation and a well-chosen sherry octave have transformed what is often used for blending into a liquid absolutely worth enjoying on its own.

103.2 proof.

A / $205

title: A Visit to the Wineries of Rioja, 2026
summary:

The post A Visit to the Wineries of Rioja, 2026 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
After our time in Bordeaux, team Drinkhacker headed south to Spain and its coastal Basque Country, posting up in the delightful town of San Sebastian. Pintxos culture couldn’t be more fun — standing in crowded bars, sipping on local txakoli wine, and chowing down on one bar snack after another. Used napkins? Tossed on the floor! It’s a lifestyle that doesn’t seem particularly healthy — rarely dining before 10pm, rarely consuming anything resembling a vegetable — but one which I could (and did) easily get used to.

From here it’s about an hour and a half to Rioja, another iconic wine region but one which is dramatically different than Bordeaux. (Along with Priorat, Rioja is one of only two DOCs in Spain.) Here, mountains hem in a sprawling, hilly valley that is absolutely covered with vines, a stark contrast to the tiny, often flat vineyards of France. The landscape is decidedly reminiscent of California, albeit even hotter.

Abutting the laconic Ebro River, wineries here measure their production in the hundreds of thousands of bottles each year, their cellars stretching seemingly forever with barrel after barrel of (mostly) tempranillo, along with smaller quantities of graciano, garnacha, maturana, and wines made from other heritage varietals. Rioja spans three regions: Rioja Alta, Rioja Alavesa, and Rioja Oreintal. All of the wineries except one that we visited were based in Rioja Alta — though many have vineyards across all three regions.

On this leg of the trip, we made our base in the town of Lagrono, which has its own pintxos scene to enjoy in the evening after a day of making the rounds to the bodegas of the region.

Unlike Bordeaux, the wineries of Rioja were very accommodating to media visits, and setting up appointments was not particularly difficult. (Thanks to the Consorzio Regulador DOCa Rioja for helping us make arrangements.) We visited a total of five spots, and I’ll tell you all about them in the writeups below.

Finca Valpiedra

Finca Valpiedra, like many wineries in Rioja, operates multiple facilities and labels, including Bujanda and Montepedroso. Tours and tastings are at the Valpiedra location, however. Our guide Paola loaded us into a Jeep to tour the terraced vineyards here, which stretch all the way down to the river’s waterfront. The massive stones that dominate the floors of the vineyard make the rocky soils of Bordeaux look like tiny pebbles. And as in Bordeaux, blazing temperatures forced the earliest harvest ever here, and harvest was well underway during our visit.

One of the most interesting parts of this vineyard tour was a close look at the Spanish practice of overgrafting, where a young vine is grafted not onto young rootstock but onto an older, healthy vine, Frankenstein-like. It’s a curious but apparently successful way to deal with the increasingly hot climate, which is hostile to young vines, while helping get the new vine to maturity much faster. It also looks slightly crazy.

We sampled three wines here — paired with local cheese and charcuterie, almost ubiquitous when tasting in the region — with a deeper dive into two Rioja offerings, a young 2022 Cantos de Valpiedra and a more mature 2018 Finca Valpiedra Reserva. This was an excellent way to get a fresh grounding on how the young joven style (very fruity with light florals) and the richer, older Reservas differ when placed side by side. The dense minerality of the Reserva was particularly bright in today’s tasting.

El Montecillo, s/n, 26360 Fuenmayor, La Rioja

Bodegas Marques de Riscal

This is probably the most visited and definitely the most photographed winery in Rioja, and it isn’t because of the wine. It’s because of a structure erected here 20 years ago that was designed by Frank Gehry. Turns out this isn’t part of the winery at all but rather a 61-room hotel, operated by Marriott. It’s quite breathtaking to behold but is certainly starting to show its age inside; the corridors particularly could use some freshening up considering the exorbitant price of staying here (typically $1000 a night and up).

The adjacent winery finds us across the Ebro in the Rioja Alavesa region, and it hosts a robust tour operation, complete with buses dropping off large groups of people who go on packed tours of a facility that turns out 10 million bottles per year. Despite the relatively impersonal nature of the tour here, it was still worthwhile and featured tastes of three wines — my favorite being a white Rueda with its green apple and gentle tropical notes. After the tour, our host offered samples of Riscal‘s 2022 Reserva XR, a special version of its Reserva designed to be softer and better balanced. Made from Riscal’s oldest vines, it’s a chewy, chocolate-heavy wine that is mostly sold in restaurants. As promised, I felt it offered a much more nuanced version of what Rioja has to offer, and was a top taste for the winery. (While not offered on the tour, you can buy a glass in the cafe.)

Calle Torrea, 1, 01340 Elciego, Araba

Bodegas Muga

Day two found us traveling to the Rioja Alta town of Haro, where some of Rioja’s best-known wineries can be found in a concentrated cluster together, all within walking distance of one another. We had a bit of a rocky start here, as our reservation had been misplaced, but after righting the situation enjoyed a lengthy and informative tour of the facility, complete with a look at its own cooperage; this is one of the only wineries in the country that produces its own vats and barrels.

Fun fact: In Spain, Muga markets its Reserva as a younger Crianza. Why? In the local market, older wines are generally shunned for fear they will be overly woody. It’s the same wine, but with a younger designation on the label, it sells better.

The typical tasting here includes just two wines, a white Rioja and Muga’s Selection Especial Reserva, but we were treated to a tasting of almost everything in the tasting room after the official tour wrapped.

This deep dive into eight additional varieties was one of the most instructive experiences I had on the trip, and I really fell in love with Muga’s 2019 Prado Enea Gran Reserva, a wildly distinctive wine with notes of licorice, slate, and nutmeg all on display atop an almost Port-like fruitiness (though sans the sweetness). Even the comparatively young 2021 Torre Muga was approachable despite its significant density; our guide Carmen suggested it would be much more refined in just six more months.

Avenida Vizcaya, Barrio de la Estación, 2, 26200 Haro, La Rioja

Bodegas La Rioja Alta

We hopped into this tasting room around the corner from Muga without an appointment because our guide suggested La Rioja Alta Gran Reserva 904 would be a fun comparison against Prado Enea. We bought a glass of the 2016 release (plus an albarino from a sister winery in Rias Baixas) and found the similarities intriguing. Lots of cocoa, currants, and some mint. A little less Port-like than Prado Enea, but quite a soulful wine to sample. Lovely grounds here, and I would have enjoyed a deeper dive into the place.

Avenida Vizcaya, 8, 26200 Haro, La Rioja

Mystery Winery

I hate to do this to you, but our final stop was at one of Rioja’s most internet-famous producers, and if you spend any time on Reddit’s r/wine boards you’ll know immediately who I’m talking about. The winery is open to visits and tastings only to media and industry professionals, and we were offered a tour on the condition that I do not write about it or post anything about the place on social media. That was a first for me, but I agreed, so I’ll leave it mostly at that. It was quite a wild tour, complete with a descent into its 150-year old cellars (pictured above) and a tasting of two of its well-aged Reservas. (2014 and 2015 are the current vintages!)

If you do figure out who I’m talking about, know that you can visit the winery’s small shop and purchase a bottle of wine (including half bottles) to take home or sip on site. Good luck!

content:
Most sourced whiskey travels a long way before it reaches the bottle. Crane Cove Rye takes a rather different route.

Brucato Spirits is a small, independent spirits company based in San Francisco’s Mission District, best known for its California-inspired amaro. With Crane Cove Rye Whiskey, part of the 2026 Distillery Series, the company ventured into whiskey while keeping its sourcing remarkably close to home. Rather than bringing in barrels from Indiana or Kentucky, Brucato sourced this whiskey from Anchor Distilling in San Francisco’s Potrero Hill neighborhood. In other words, this may be a sourced whiskey, but it is very much a San Francisco whiskey.

There is another detail that makes Crane Cove Rye stand apart: the mashbill is 100% malted rye. The grain, sourced from Briess Malting in Wisconsin and grown in the upper Midwest, underwent a two-day upward step fermentation using Anchor Brewing’s ale yeast. The fermentation produced considerable foam and a wort around 9% ABV. Anchor also left the spent grain with the liquid during distillation rather than separating the two beforehand.

The resulting distillate went through double copper pot distillation on a 1,500-liter wash still and a 700-liter spirit still fitted with an agitator. On January 13, 2017, the distillate entered two 53-gallon Cooper’s Reserve barrels at 123.9 proof. Those barrels were eventually dumped in the second half of June 2026, giving the whiskey nine years and five months of maturation.

The barrels themselves were no ordinary containers. Made by Independent Stave Company from fine-grain American white oak, they were open-air seasoned for 24 months, given a #3 char over an oak scrap fire, and subjected to a heavy toast. The Cooper’s Reserve barrels cost roughly four times as much as a standard distillery barrel. After the two barrels were blended, the whiskey came out at its natural harvest proof of 129.

For a small San Francisco spirits company, there is plenty here to set Crane Cove Rye apart from the usual sourced-whiskey story: local distillation, 100% malted rye, ale yeast fermentation, copper pot distillation, nearly a decade in Cooper’s Reserve barrels, and a final proof of 129.

Is this unusual San Francisco rye whiskey worthy of attention beyond the confines of Bay Area locals? Let’s find out.

Brucato Spirits Crane Cove Rye 9 Years Old Review

The nose starts with plenty of juicy, ripe fruit, led by freshly sliced cantaloupe and white grape juice. As the fruit settles, honey graham crackers bring a sweet, bready aroma alongside milk chocolate. For those encountering malted rye for the first time, it is worth comparing it with the much more common unmalted rye whiskey that remains the industry standard. The malting process tends to yield rye whiskey that is soft, fruity, and floral, and all three qualities are readily apparent on the nose.

The palate starts with less-sweet wild blackberries before moving into pine needles. The mid-palate turns spicy with clove, followed by a familiar dill note and a very dense mouthfeel. The finish moves toward a more traditional rye profile, with white pepper joining stewed green apple, followed by another push of clove and a final touch of cocoa powder.

Overall, this is a beautiful example of malted rye whiskey. I tend to gravitate toward rye whiskey in general, in large part because of the diversity the category offers, and malted rye remains an underrepresented style within the category. This is the longest-aged malted rye I have experienced, and I am very pleased with the result. Even after nine years in new charred oak barrels, the fruity qualities of the malted rye grain remain clearly present.

110 proof.

B+ / $99
